title: ‘Look past headline returns’: ASIC urges trustees to up private credit diligence
full_text:
ASIC commissioner Simone Constant has flagged how exposed super fund members are to private markets and their associated risks.
Speaking at the Commercial & Asset Finance Brokers of Australia (CAFBA) Commercial Property & Development Finance Summit in Sydney on 22 September, ASIC commissioner Simone Constant said the watchdog had shone a light on weaknesses in private credit.
A risk of this for super members is the potential for fund gatings or lock-up periods if a private credit fund comes into trouble or events like the recent collapse of property developer Bathla which can leave superannuation members unable to access a portion of their savings.
“Millions of Australians are exposed to private credit – some through direct fund investment, others through shares in private credit fund managers, but many through their superannuation fund.
“Now, where superannuation funds allocate assets prudently and where the private credit investments themselves are done well, this is a great thing for investors, borrowers and the economy.
“But against the backdrop of super’s significant growth in funds under management and what feels like exponential growth in private credit, ASIC’s focus on the sector should come as no surprise.
“When there is too much inconsistency in standards in a market of this scale, ASIC will maintain and continue to sharpen our focus on the sector.”
Constant warned super funds and fund trustees cannot use private credit in the same way as traditional fixed income assets or view it as a “high-yielding substitute” even if the headlines are attractive. It also requires stricter due diligence and questioning of managers especially as private markets is an asset class with high differential between the performance of fund managers.
It is also up to super trustees to be the leaders in driving best practice and meeting ASIC’s 10 best practice principles given the billions of assets they manage on behalf of Australians.
“Trustees have clear statutory obligations to act in their members’ best financial interests. Fulfilling that duty requires genuine, look-through due diligence.
“Trustees must look past the headline returns, examine the underlying collateral, verify the bad-debt provisioning, and independently test those manager assumptions before committing member capital.
“It actually really continues to surprise me when CIOs of very large, sophisticated trustee funds are reluctant to ask their own fund managers whether they’re meeting our 10 principles of “private credit done well”, and this is especially the case when most of those principles can be extended more universally across private markets and when actually, most of those standards are what we think those trustees already expect of themselves.”
author: Laura Dew
heading: Superannuation and Investments
